fields.meta_title: How to Walk in Humility (and Overcome Pride)
fields.description: Humility is the soil of every virtue and pride the root of every sin. Here is how to grow in humility — by looking to Christ, serving others, and receiving God’s grace.
fields.body_html:
Humility is the soil in which every other virtue grows, and pride is the root of nearly every sin. Yet humility is strangely elusive: the moment we think we have attained it, we have lost it. It cannot be worked up by effort or worn as a pose; it is the quiet fruit of seeing ourselves, God, and others truly. Scripture makes humility not optional but essential, for it stands at the very centre of how God deals with us: “God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble” (James 4:6). To grow in humility is to position ourselves under the flow of God’s grace; to indulge pride is to set ourselves against him. Here is how to walk the humble path.

Why humility matters so much

The stakes could not be higher. Twice the Bible states the same law of the spiritual world: “God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble” (1 Peter 5:5). Pride puts us on the wrong side of God himself, while humility opens the channel of his grace. This alone should sober us, for pride is the most deceptive of sins — it hides from the very person who has it, dressing itself up as confidence, or principle, or wounded dignity.

Pride was the first sin and remains the deadliest, for “pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall” (Proverbs 16:18). It lies beneath our conflicts, our defensiveness, our craving for recognition, our inability to admit fault. Humility is its cure. Where pride isolates and destroys, humility heals and builds. And the promise attached to it is sweet: “Humble yourselves, therefore, under the mighty hand of God so that at the proper time he may exalt you” (1 Peter 5:6). The way up, in God’s kingdom, is always down.

Look to Jesus, the humble King

Humility is learned not chiefly by trying but by looking — looking at Jesus. The Lord of glory, who had every right to be served, “emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant” and “humbled himself by becoming obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross” (Philippians 2:7–8). The King of heaven washed his disciples’ feet and said, “I have given you an example, that you also should do just as I have done to you” (John 13:14–15). No one who truly beholds the humility of Christ can remain comfortably proud.

So the surest path to humility is to fill our gaze with him. “Have this mind among yourselves, which is yours in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 2:5). As we contemplate his descent — from the throne to the manger, from the manger to the cross — our own self-importance begins to look absurd. Pride cannot survive long in the presence of the crucified God. Look at him often, and humility will grow in you almost without your noticing.

See yourself truly — before God

Humility is not thinking badly of ourselves; it is thinking honestly, in the light of God. It is seeing that all we have is a gift, that we are sinners saved by grace, that we depend on God for our very breath. Paul counsels, “by the grace given to me I say to everyone among you not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think, but to think with sober judgment” (Romans 12:3). Humility is sober self-assessment, neither inflated nor falsely lowered.

The great leveller is the cross. There we see both how sinful we are — that it took the death of the Son of God to save us — and how loved we are, that he was willing to die. This double truth kills pride at the root. We have nothing to boast in, for we brought nothing but our sin; and we have nothing to prove, for we are already loved. The humble person has stopped both the exhausting work of self-promotion and the equally exhausting work of self-loathing, and has found rest in simply being a forgiven child of God.

Put others first

Humility shows itself most clearly in how we treat other people. It is not merely a private feeling but a way of relating: “Do nothing from selfish ambition or conceit, but in humility count others more significant than yourselves. Let each of you look not only to his own interests, but also to the interests of others” (Philippians 2:3–4). The humble person makes room for others, celebrates their gifts without envy, and serves without needing to be noticed.

This is intensely practical. It means listening more than we speak, admitting when we are wrong, giving credit generously, and taking the lowly task no one else wants. Jesus taught it plainly: “When you are invited, go and sit in the lowest place”, for “everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 14:10–11). Stop competing for the highest seat, and let God do any exalting he sees fit. The one who serves quietly, seeks no applause, and lifts others up is walking the very road Jesus walked.

Learn to spot pride at work

Because pride is so good at hiding, it helps to know its usual disguises. Pride shows itself in defensiveness — the inability to take criticism without excusing ourselves. It shows in comparison, whether we come away feeling superior or bitterly inferior. It shows in a craving for recognition, a wounded touchiness when overlooked, a reluctance to apologize, a habit of steering conversations back to ourselves. It hides even in false humility, which fishes for compliments by running itself down. Jesus warned that “everyone who exalts himself will be humbled” (Matthew 23:12), and much self-exalting is quiet and respectable.

Naming these patterns is not meant to plunge us into self-loathing but to bring pride into the light where grace can deal with it. When we notice ourselves getting defensive, envious, or hungry for praise, we can pause and turn it into a prayer: “Lord, there is my pride again; forgive me, and give me the lowly heart of your Son.” The very ability to see our pride is itself a mercy, for the proudest state of all is to imagine we have no pride left. Honest self-awareness, held before God, is the soil in which humility quietly grows.

Embrace the humbling God allows

God is committed to making us humble, and in his kindness he often arranges circumstances that expose our pride and bring us low. Failures, corrections, disappointments, and the honest words of others are frequently his tools. The humble response is not to resent these but to receive them, asking what God would teach us. “Humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God” (1 Peter 5:6) sometimes means simply accepting the humbling he permits, rather than fighting to protect our dignity.

This is hard, because pride recoils from being corrected or overlooked. But every such moment is an invitation to die a little more to self and to grow in the grace God gives the lowly. When we are criticized, we can ask whether there is truth to learn rather than rushing to defend ourselves. When we are passed over, we can rejoice that our worth rests in God, not in recognition. The humbling that stings today is often the making of us tomorrow, for God is a faithful teacher who loves us too much to leave us proud.

Ask God for a humble heart

Finally, because humility cannot be manufactured by willpower, we must ask God for it. It is his gift, worked in us by his Spirit, and we should seek it earnestly in prayer. The old saints understood that the pursuit of humility is a lifelong work, never finished this side of heaven — but one God delights to advance in those who ask. What he requires, he also supplies: “He has told you, O man, what is good... to do justice, and to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God” (Micah 6:8).

So make it your daily prayer: “Lord, make me humble; show me my pride; give me the mind of Christ.” Look often at Jesus, serve the people around you, receive correction gladly, and refuse to grasp for recognition. Humility will not come all at once, and the moment you congratulate yourself on it, you will have to begin again. But God gives grace to the humble, and every step down into lowliness is a step deeper into that grace — and, in the end, the way home to the God who humbled himself for us. Take heart, too, in the promise attached to the whole pursuit: the God who resists the proud delights to lift up the lowly. “He who humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 14:11). We need not scramble for honour or defend our place; we can take the lowest seat and leave any raising to God, who has never yet forgotten a humble servant. The truly humble are the truly free — free from the exhausting need to be seen, to be right, to be first — and that freedom is one of the sweetest fruits of walking humbly with God.
